/lists/best-books-for-new-managers/.title: Start managing a team
/lists/best-books-for-new-managers/.need: Move from doing the work yourself to enabling other people, with useful first conversations and clear commitments.
/lists/best-books-for-new-managers/.selectionOrderReason: A role model, a practical tool reference, a day-to-day coaching habit, then a team-dynamics lens. This is a reading sequence, not an empirical book ranking.
/lists/best-books-for-new-managers/.overlapDecision: Use this existing, specific destination. /lists/best-books-for-first-time-leaders/ has the same generic selections and much weaker impressions; hold that duplicate out of indexing or consolidate only after the destination contains the repaired journey. Keep the broader leadership guide distinct.

choices.bookAuthor: Tacy Byham and Richard S. Wellins

choices.limitations: The review covers many tasks briefly; it does not substitute for training, policy or employment advice.

choices.whyThisFits: The contributor explains how seven coaching questions keep ownership with the person bringing the problem.

choices.limitations: Use coaching when someone can discover an answer; urgent instruction or a necessary decision still needs a manager.
choices.readerAction: Use one of the seven original coaching questions in a suitable one-to-one.

choices.limitations: It is a business fable and framework. Structural, workload or misconduct issues are not always a trust problem.

/lists/best-communication-books/.title: Prepare for a difficult conversation
/lists/best-communication-books/.need: Notice your assumptions, understand the other person, and discuss specific behaviour without turning honesty into aggression.
/lists/best-communication-books/.selectionOrderReason: Prepare your own mindset, create shared meaning, balance honesty and compassion, then structure performance feedback.
/lists/best-communication-books/.overlapDecision: Add this focused path to the existing communication list. Do not create another competing guide solely for a keyword variation. Public speaking and sales picks can remain separate labelled needs only if their fit is individually substantiated.

choices.book: Change Your Questions, Change Your Life
choices.whyThisFits: Alison Spitzer gives the Learner/Judger distinction, ABCC prompts and twelve questions, including what assumptions you are making.
choices.exactOriginalExcerpt: The author outlines two paths, or mindsets: Learner and Judger.
choices.limitations: This changes how the reader approaches a conversation; it is not a guarantee that the other person will cooperate.
choices.readerAction: Try the original ABCC prompts before a difficult conversation.
choices.bookAuthorBasis: Named author from the restored review and corresponding archive author record; no claim of newly verified author biography.

choices.bookAuthor: Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler
choices.whyThisFits: The original explains the pool of shared meaning and how people attach stories to facts.
choices.readerSituation: Get facts, stories and concerns into shared view
choices.exactOriginalExcerpt: Crucial conversations are only resolved effectively when others in the conversation are made aware of, and understand, our stories, facts, and emotions.
choices.limitations: The review covers an earlier edition. Its historical physiology explanation is simplified, and one page reference contains an unresolved typo.
choices.readerAction: Separate observable facts from the stories attached to them, and ask what each person wants from the relationship.
choices.bookAuthorBasis: Use the original four-author edition. The current archive metadata names only Al Switzler. A later edition includes Emily Gregory; do not silently substitute its author list.

choices.whyThisFits: The contributor explicitly warns that honesty does not justify blunt statements without considering their effect.
choices.exactOriginalExcerpt: Digging deeper and being honest does not give you the right to simply unload blunt statements on the other person and end it there
choices.limitations: Power, safety and workplace duties still matter. The framework is not permission for abusive confrontation.
choices.readerAction: Prepare one honest, compassionate question and leave space for the other person's perspective.
choices.bookAuthorBasis: Named author from the restored review and corresponding archive author record; no claim of newly verified author biography.

choices.whyThisFits: The review lays out observations, feelings, needs and requests for discussing unhelpful behaviour.

choices.limitations: The approach helps frame a conversation. It does not replace judgment about workload, trust or the other person’s willingness to participate.
choices.readerAction: Prepare observations, feelings, needs and a clear request for a real performance conversation.
